Coeur d'Alene Tribe

The Coeur d'Alene Tribe is an Idaho tribal government whose public histories connect community, land and water. This starting guide follows the Tribe's own accounts of historical change, language documentation and care for the lake. The wider Coeur d'Alene reading profile supplies additional context without replacing this named government route.

Seltice, Chief of the Coeur D’Alênes, 1891
Olin Levi Warner, 1891. Smithsonian American Art Museum, A Gift of Alison Warner Waterman in memory of her mother, Frances D. Warner, 1985.76.3. Public domain.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — SAAM item marked Free to use

Museum photograph of Olin Levi Warner’s 1891 bronze portrait relief of the specifically identified Coeur d’Alene leader Seltice. This is an outside sculptor’s historical portrait, not Coeur d’Alene-made art, a photograph of the living sitter, or a present government representation. The museum’s curators place Warner’s portraits in the context of racial classification and an erroneous expectation that Native peoples would disappear, and note that the sitters’ perspectives are poorly documented. That context is retained; no essential cultural or physical trait is inferred from the portrait. No traditional design meanings or community endorsement are claimed. These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Community history and land

The Tribe's history introduces place, naming, government and changes in land ownership through a community-published account. It provides an opening perspective on relationships disrupted by settlement and land loss. Its acreage and chronology need comparison with the underlying agreements and records before making detailed legal claims. This narrative belongs to the Tribe; it does not summarize every neighboring Salish community.

Read the sources [1] Coeur d’Alene Tribe

02

Named work in language documentation

The Culture Department describes a 1973 documentation effort and credits Lawrence G. Nicodemus and Joseph N. Bitar with work on writing and documenting the Coeur d'Alene language. Its reading-and-writing article combines a community history of that work with alphabet and lesson material. These public resources offer a concrete way into language learning while leaving present fluency and teaching outcomes unmeasured.

Read the sources [2] Coeur d’Alene Tribe, Culture Department

03

The lake and a dated environmental account

The Tribe's lake-management account links water with spiritual and material life, and discusses mining pollution, management planning and hydropower licensing. Several conditions and procedural details are explicitly dated to 2005. Read it as the Tribe's environmental history and perspective, then seek newer records for current cleanup conditions.

Read the sources [3] Coeur d’Alene Tribe
